question: A 78-year-old male comes to the physician’s office for a routine check-up. He complains of increased lower extremity swelling, inability to climb the one flight of stairs in his home, and waking up in the middle of the night 2-3 times gasping for breath. He has had to increase the number of pillows on which he sleeps at night. These symptoms started 9 months ago and have been progressing. The doctor starts him on a medication regimen, one of which changes his Starling curve from A to B as shown in the Figure. Which of the following medications is most consistent with this mechanism of action?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Increased lower extremity swelling -> decreased cardiac output -> increased preload -> changes Starling curve from A to B -> Furosemide -> 95%
CHAIN: Inability to climb stairs -> decreased exercise tolerance -> decreased cardiac function -> increased preload -> changes Starling curve from A to B -> Furosemide -> 90%
CHAIN: Waking up gasping for breath -> paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea -> pulmonary congestion -> increased preload -> changes Starling curve from A to B -> Furosemide -> 90%
CHAIN: Needing more pillows to sleep -> orthopnea -> pulmonary congestion -> increased preload -> changes Starling curve from A to B -> Furosemide -> 90%
enhanced_information: The medication most consistent with the mechanism of action described, changing the Starling curve from A to B by reducing preload, is Furosemide. This aligns with the patient's symptoms of increased lower extremity swelling, inability to climb stairs, waking up gasping for breath, and needing more pillows to sleep due to pulmonary congestion and increased preload. The evidence path confirming orthopnea as a manifestation of pulmonary congestion supports the choice of Furosemide.
analysis: The patient's symptoms of lower extremity swelling, dyspnea, orthopnea, and increased preload suggest heart failure. The medication that changes the Starling curve by reducing preload is Furosemide, a loop diuretic commonly used in heart failure to reduce fluid overload and congestion.
